quests.instruction: In “Maya bought some bread yesterday”, which words carry the main beats?
quests.word: Maya bought some bread yesterday
quests.textToSpeak: Maya bought some bread yesterday
options: “Maya”, “bought”, “bread” and “yesterday”: the content words
“Maya”, “some” and “yesterday”: the first and last words plus “some”
Every word equally, one beat each
Only “bought” and “some”: the verb and its small neighbour
quests.correctAnswer: “Maya”, “bought”, “bread” and “yesterday”: the content words
quests.hint: Tap the rhythm of the sentence as you say it. Which words make you tap, and which fall between the taps?
quests.explanation: English rhythm tends to place the main beats on the words that carry the meaning: names, main verbs, nouns and adverbs. The small words, such as “some”, fall quietly between them. So the sentence is heard as “MAya BOUGHT some BREAD YESterday”.
quests.phoneticRule: Content words typically carry the stressed beats of a sentence, while function words fill the gaps between beats.

quests.instruction: English rhythm tends to place stressed syllables at roughly even intervals. What does that mean for the small words in “Zane sent a text to the team”?
quests.word: Zane sent a text to the team
quests.textToSpeak: Zane sent a text to the team
options: They are stretched so that every word in the sentence takes exactly the same time
They are dropped completely, so only the content words remain in the speech
They are stressed too, to keep the beats even across the whole sentence
They are squeezed into the gaps between stressed words and become short and weak in speech
quests.correctAnswer: They are squeezed into the gaps between stressed words and become short and weak in speech
quests.hint: Count the stressed words, then notice how little time is left for the words between them.
quests.explanation: Roughly speaking, the time between beats stays similar, so the small words between “sent”, “text” and “team” are crammed into short gaps. They become brief and weak: “ZANE SENT uh TEXT tuh thuh TEAM”. This is a tendency, not a strict rule, but it explains why small words seem to vanish.
quests.phoneticRule: English is described as stress-timed: stressed syllables tend to recur at roughly regular intervals, so the unstressed syllables between them are compressed.
quests.spokenForm: ZANE SENT uh TEXT tuh thuh TEAM

quests.instruction: Which words fall between the beats in “Ivan found a note on the desk”?
quests.word: Ivan found a note on the desk
quests.textToSpeak: Ivan found a note on the desk
options: “found”, “note” and “desk”, which are the least important words
“a”, “on” and “the”, which are squeezed between the beats
“Ivan” and “found”, which are the first two words
None: all words are equally squeezed
quests.correctAnswer: “a”, “on” and “the”, which are squeezed between the beats
quests.hint: Find the words that carry the information, then see what is left.
quests.explanation: The beats fall on “Ivan”, “found”, “note” and “desk”. The three small words, “a”, “on” and “the”, are squeezed between them and are pronounced weakly: /ə/, /ɒn/ and /ðə/. The same method works for any sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: Identifying the stressed content words leaves the function words that are compressed between the beats.
quests.spokenForm: IVan FOUND uh NOTE on thuh DESK

quests.instruction: Which sentence takes about the same time to say naturally as “Cats sit on mats”?
quests.word: Cats sit on mats
quests.textToSpeak: Cats sit on mats
options: “Cats sit on mats, and dogs sit on rugs”, with six stressed words
“The cats are sitting on the mats”, with three stressed words
“The big black cats sat on the mats”, with five stressed words
“Cats sit”, with two stressed words
quests.correctAnswer: “The cats are sitting on the mats”, with three stressed words
quests.hint: Count the stressed words in each sentence rather than the number of syllables.
quests.explanation: Because the beats tend to come at even intervals, the number of stressed words matters more than the number of syllables. “Cats sit on mats” and “The cats are sitting on the mats” both have three beats, so the longer sentence squeezes its extra small words into the gaps. The other options have more or fewer beats.
quests.phoneticRule: Sentence duration in English depends mainly on the number of stressed syllables, not on the total number of syllables.

quests.instruction: “Nora wants to buy a hat” and “Nora wants to buy hats” take almost the same time to say. Why?
quests.word: Nora wants to buy a hat
quests.textToSpeak: Nora wants to buy a hat
options: The speaker talks faster on every word of the longer sentence to catch up
The extra word is dropped in speech, so the sentences are identical
Spoken English gives every word one beat, so the lengths match exactly
The extra word “a” is unstressed, so it is squeezed between two beats
quests.correctAnswer: The extra word “a” is unstressed, so it is squeezed between two beats
quests.hint: Look at the one word that the longer sentence adds, and decide whether it takes a beat.
quests.explanation: Both sentences have the same stressed words (Nora, wants, buy, hat or hats), and the extra word in the longer one is unstressed. It shares the time between the beats, so the longer sentence needs almost no extra time. The effect is a tendency, not an exact measure.
quests.phoneticRule: Adding an unstressed function word to a sentence adds little time because it is compressed within the interval between stressed syllables.
quests.spokenForm: NOra WANTS tuh BUY uh HAT

quests.instruction: Which pattern describes the rhythm of “Rita bought bread and milk”?
quests.word: Rita bought bread and milk
quests.textToSpeak: Rita bought bread and milk
options: Five beats, with “and” stressed like all the other content words
Four beats: Rita, bought, bread and milk, with “and” squeezed in
Two beats: only the first word and the last word are stressed
Six beats, one for each syllable of the whole sentence
quests.correctAnswer: Four beats: Rita, bought, bread and milk, with “and” squeezed in
quests.hint: Tap the beats on the words you would underline, and see how “and” fits between taps.
quests.explanation: “Rita”, “bought”, “bread” and “milk” are the meaning words and take the beats. “And” is reduced to a short /n/ and fits into the gap between “bread” and “milk”. Hearing four beats and one squeezed word is the typical pattern in lists.
quests.phoneticRule: In lists, content words carry the beats and the conjunction “and” is compressed into the interval between them.

quests.instruction: Which rhythm pattern fits “Drop me a line”?
quests.word: Drop me a line
quests.textToSpeak: Drop me a line
options: DROP ME A LINE: four equal beats, one for each word
drop ME a line: the main beat falls on “me”
DROP me a LINE: two beats, with “me a” squeezed in between them
DROP me A LINE: three beats, with “a” and “line” both stressed
quests.correctAnswer: DROP me a LINE: two beats, with “me a” squeezed in between them
quests.hint: Say the phrase as a quick request and tap the beats.
quests.explanation: “Drop me a line” has two content words, “drop” and “line”, so it has two beats. The words “me a” are squeezed between them: “DROP muh uh LINE”. A learner who gives all four words the same weight sounds slow and may hide the key words.
quests.phoneticRule: Short requests have one beat per content word, with pronouns and articles squeezed between them.

quests.instruction: In “Olga, pass me a pen”, how many beats are there, and where do they fall?
quests.word: Olga, pass me a pen
quests.textToSpeak: Olga, pass me a pen
options: Five beats, one for each of the five words in the sentence
Two beats on pass and pen only, with no beat on the name
Three beats on Olga, pass and pen, with “me a” squeezed
Four beats on Olga, pass, me and pen, with “a” squeezed
quests.correctAnswer: Three beats on Olga, pass and pen, with “me a” squeezed
quests.hint: Count the words you would stress if you were asking quickly across a table.
quests.explanation: A name, the verb and the noun carry the beats: “OLga, PASS muh uh PEN”. “Me” and “a” are small and are squeezed into the gap after “pass”. The sentence is therefore three beats long, and it takes about as long as other three-beat sentences.
quests.phoneticRule: A vocative name counts as a beat, and the pronoun and article that follow a verb are compressed.

quests.instruction: Which pattern fits “Keep me posted”?
quests.word: Keep me posted
quests.textToSpeak: Keep me posted
options: KEEP ME POSTED: three even beats, one for each word
KEEP me POSTed: two beats, with “me” squeezed in the gap
keep ME POSTed: the main beat falls on “me” and “posted”
KEEP me posted: the last word is squeezed
quests.correctAnswer: KEEP me POSTed: two beats, with “me” squeezed in the gap
quests.hint: Say it the way you would end a conversation, and notice which two words carry the weight.
quests.explanation: “Keep” and “posted” carry the meaning, so they take the beats, and the pronoun “me” is squeezed between them: “KEEP mi POSTed”. The rhythm of the phrase is two beats, however short or long the words in between are.
quests.phoneticRule: A pronoun between a verb and its complement is typically unstressed and compressed between the two beats.

quests.instruction: Which words carry the beats in “Maya, what time are you free?”
quests.word: Maya, what time are you free
quests.textToSpeak: Maya, what time are you free
options: “Maya”, “what” and “you”: the shortest words
Every word equally, with no squeezed words at all
Only “what” and “free”: the first and last question words
“Maya”, “time” and “free”; the other words are squeezed
quests.correctAnswer: “Maya”, “time” and “free”; the other words are squeezed
quests.hint: Think about which words the listener needs to catch: the time and the person, not the small grammar words.
quests.explanation: In a neutral question the stress falls on “time” and “free”, and on the vocative “Maya”. The words “what”, “are” and “you” are squeezed between: “MAya, wot TIME uh yuh FREE”. Hearing the beats first makes it easier to catch the question even when the small words blur.
quests.phoneticRule: In wh-questions, the stress falls on the content words, while the wh-word and following function words are weak or squeezed.
quests.spokenForm: MAya, wot TIME uh yuh FREE

quests.instruction: Why do “is” and “the” almost vanish in “Farid, where’s the nearest station?”
quests.word: Farid, where’s the nearest station
quests.textToSpeak: Farid, where’s the nearest station
options: They are stressed to keep the rhythm even
They are unstressed words squeezed between the beats on “nearest” and “station”
They are replaced by weak vowels only in very careful speech, and kept strong otherwise
They are dropped because the question is short
quests.correctAnswer: They are unstressed words squeezed between the beats on “nearest” and “station”
quests.hint: Find the stressed words in the question and look at what is left between them.
quests.explanation: “Nearest” and “station” carry the beats. “Where’s the” is the stretch in front of them, and it is compressed: “wheres thuh”. The contraction “where’s” also makes the stretch shorter. So the speaker can say the long sentence at the same pace as a short one.
quests.phoneticRule: Contracted and unstressed function words are compressed into the intervals between stressed syllables, so long questions do not necessarily take longer.

quests.instruction: Which question matches the quick rhythm “ROsa, how-LONG-iz-thuh-FILM”?
quests.word: Rosa, how long is the film
quests.textToSpeak: Rosa, how long is the film
options: “Rosa, how long was the film?”
“Rosa, how long is a film?”
“Rosa, how long are the films?”
“Rosa, how long is the film?”
quests.correctAnswer: “Rosa, how long is the film?”
quests.hint: Listen to the small words between the stressed ones: is, the, a, was, are.
quests.explanation: The stressed words are the same in every option, so the small words must be decoded: “iz” is “is” and “thuh” is “the”. “Was” would be /wəz/ and “a” would be /ə/. Using the beats as an anchor and then filling in the small words is a good decoding strategy.
quests.phoneticRule: Decoding fast speech: locate the stressed beats first, then identify the weak words by their reduced vowels and consonants.
quests.spokenForm: ROsa, how LONG iz thuh FILM

quests.instruction: Compare “Anya sent him a letter” with “Anya sent HIM a letter”. What changes in the second?
quests.word: Anya sent him a letter
quests.textToSpeak: Anya sent him a letter
options: “sent” is reduced to /sənt/, because it comes before “HIM”
Nothing changes: stress does not affect the form of pronouns in speech
“letter” loses its stress, because “him” takes all of it
“him” is stressed, so it keeps a full vowel and /h/: /hɪm/, not /ɪm/
quests.correctAnswer: “him” is stressed, so it keeps a full vowel and /h/: /hɪm/, not /ɪm/
quests.hint: Ask which word the speaker wants you to notice in the second sentence.
quests.explanation: Stress changes which words are reduced. In the neutral sentence, “him” is weak and often loses its /h/: /ɪm/. When the speaker stresses it, to show it was him and not someone else, it keeps its /h/ and full vowel: /hɪm/. The words around it stay the same.
quests.phoneticRule: Contrastive stress converts a weak pronoun into a strong form, so the same words can have different reductions depending on focus.

quests.instruction: In “Ravi walked to the station, not from it”, which form of “to” is likely?
quests.word: Ravi walked to the station, not from it
quests.textToSpeak: Ravi walked to the station, not from it
options: /tə/, because prepositions take weak forms even when contrasted
/tʊ/ before “the”, as before a vowel sound such as “eat”
/tuː/, a full vowel, because “to” is contrasted with “from”
/də/ with a voiced /t/, as in a casual tap
quests.correctAnswer: /tuː/, a full vowel, because “to” is contrasted with “from”
quests.hint: Ask whether “to” is part of the background or the point of the sentence.
quests.explanation: Normally “to” is weak, /tə/. Here the speaker contrasts “to” with “from”, so “to” is stressed and returns to its strong form /tuː/. The surrounding words keep their usual reductions.
quests.phoneticRule: Stress on a preposition in a contrast restores its strong form, even though the weak form is the default.
quests.spokenForm: RAvi WALKED TOO the STAtion, not FROM it

quests.instruction: Someone asks, “Did Leo or Jake call?” You answer, “Leo called.” Which word carries the main beat?
quests.word: Leo called, not Jake
quests.textToSpeak: Leo called, not Jake
options: “Leo”, because it is the new information
“called”, because verbs take the main stress
Both words equally
Neither: the answer is reduced
quests.correctAnswer: “Leo”, because it is the new information
quests.hint: The question already contains “call”. Which part of the answer is new?
quests.explanation: The new information is who called, so “Leo” takes the main beat, and “called” is given less prominence because the question already mentioned it. This shows that stress follows information, not word class.
quests.phoneticRule: Stress falls on the new or contrasted information; given information is typically de-accented.

quests.instruction: Which description fits “black coffee” in “Order a black coffee”?
quests.word: Order a black coffee
quests.textToSpeak: Order a black coffee
options: One longer /k/: the closure is held, then released once
Two separate /k/ sounds, each released clearly
The /k/ is dropped completely, so only “bla-offee” remains
The /k/ becomes a /g/ in the middle
quests.correctAnswer: One longer /k/: the closure is held, then released once
quests.hint: Say “black coffee” and notice what your tongue does between the two /k/ sounds.
quests.explanation: “Black” ends in /k/ and “coffee” begins with /k/. Instead of making two separate stops, speakers hold one closure and release it once, so you hear a single, slightly longer /k/. This is gemination. The two words are still both present; the boundary is simply less obvious.
quests.phoneticRule: Gemination: when two identical consonants meet across a word boundary, they are usually realised as one longer consonant with a single release.

quests.instruction: Which sound is lengthened in “some more” in “Add some more sugar”?
quests.word: Add some more sugar
quests.textToSpeak: Add some more sugar
options: The vowel /ʌ/ of “some”, which is held for a longer time
The /s/ at the start of “some”, which is held for longer
The /m/: the lips stay closed for one longer /m/
The vowel /ɔː/ of “more”, which becomes much longer
quests.correctAnswer: The /m/: the lips stay closed for one longer /m/
quests.hint: Both words meet at the same lip sound. What happens to your lips between the two?
quests.explanation: “Some” ends in /m/ and “more” begins with /m/. The lips stay closed, and the nasal is held a little longer: /sʌmːɔː/. You do not hear a separate /m/ for each word, so “some more” can sound like “sumore”.
quests.phoneticRule: Identical nasals across a boundary merge into a single lengthened nasal, so the closure is not released between them.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “ten numbers” fits “Pick ten numbers”?
quests.word: Pick ten numbers
quests.textToSpeak: Pick ten numbers
options: Two /n/ sounds separated by a short vowel
One longer /n/: “te-nnumbers”
The /n/ is dropped: “te-umbers”
The first /n/ becomes /m/
quests.correctAnswer: One longer /n/: “te-nnumbers”
quests.hint: Both words meet at an /n/; notice whether your tongue leaves the ridge between them.
quests.explanation: “Ten” ends in /n/ and “numbers” begins with /n/, so the tongue stays on the ridge and the nasal is held a little longer: “te-nnumbers”. A listener who expects two clear /n/ sounds may find it hard to hear the boundary at first.
quests.phoneticRule: Gemination applies to all identical consonants, and the held nasal is typically longer than a single nasal.

quests.instruction: What is heard where “bus” and “stop” meet in “Nora lives near the bus stop”?
quests.word: Nora lives near the bus stop
quests.textToSpeak: Nora lives near the bus stop
options: Two separate /s/ sounds with a pause between them
The /s/ of “bus” is dropped completely
The /s/ becomes a /z/ before “stop”
One longer /s/: the hiss is held before the /t/ starts
quests.correctAnswer: One longer /s/: the hiss is held before the /t/ starts
quests.hint: Both words contribute an /s/ at the boundary. Do you hear one hiss or two?
quests.explanation: “Bus” ends in /s/ and “stop” begins with /s/ plus /t/. The hiss is held as one longer /s/ before the /t/ starts: “bus-sstop”. The words are not run together beyond recognition; the held /s/ is itself a clue that two /s/ sounds meet.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final fricative followed by an identical word-initial fricative is realised as a single lengthened fricative.

quests.instruction: Why does the /t/ in “that time” sound longer than a normal /t/ in “Remember that time we got lost”?
quests.word: Remember that time we got lost
quests.textToSpeak: Remember that time we got lost
options: The /t/ is voiced, so it lasts longer than a voiceless /t/
“that” is stressed, which doubles every sound
Two identical /t/ sounds meet: one closure, one release
A vowel is inserted between the two /t/ sounds
quests.correctAnswer: Two identical /t/ sounds meet: one closure, one release
quests.hint: Count how many separate releases of air you can feel in “that time”.
quests.explanation: “That” ends in /t/ and “time” begins with /t/. The tongue closes once, holds the closure, and releases once, so you hear one long /t/. This is why “that time” does not sound like two /t/ sounds. Many learners insert a break instead, which sounds heavier.
quests.phoneticRule: Identical stops across a boundary are realised with one held closure and a single release, so the closure is lengthened.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “big game” fits “Big game tonight”?
quests.word: Big game tonight
quests.textToSpeak: Big game tonight
options: “big … game”: two separate /g/ sounds with a pause
“bi-ame”: the /g/ is dropped
“bi-kgame”: the first /g/ becomes /k/
“bi-ggame”: one longer /g/ with a single release
quests.correctAnswer: “bi-ggame”: one longer /g/ with a single release
quests.hint: Say “big game” fast and notice how many times your tongue releases the /g/.
quests.explanation: “Big” ends in /g/ and “game” begins with /g/. The back of the tongue stays up for a moment longer and releases once: “bi-ggame”. The same pattern applies to /b b/, /d d/, /p p/ and others across word boundaries.
quests.phoneticRule: Gemination applies to voiced stops as well as voiceless stops: the closure is held and released once.

quests.instruction: Which beats and links are heard in “Mia, wait for it at the door”?
quests.word: Mia, wait for it at the door
quests.textToSpeak: Mia, wait for it at the door
options: Three beats (Mia, wait, door); “for it at the” is squeezed and linked
Seven even beats, one per word, with no squeezed words and no links
Five beats, with “for” and “at” stressed as prepositions normally are
Two beats, with all small words dropped from the sentence completely
quests.correctAnswer: Three beats (Mia, wait, door); “for it at the” is squeezed and linked
quests.hint: Find the stressed words first, then look for consonant-vowel boundaries among the small words.
quests.explanation: The beats fall on “Mia”, “wait” and “door”. Between “wait” and “door”, the small words “for it at the” are compressed and linked: a linking /r/ after “for” and the /t/ of “it” onto “at”. So rhythm and linking work together to make the sentence flow.
quests.phoneticRule: In a longer chunk, rhythm compresses the function words and linking joins them, so the two features occur at the same time.

quests.instruction: Which words are linked and which are stressed in “Dana, pick it up and go home”?
quests.word: Dana, pick it up and go home
quests.textToSpeak: Dana, pick it up and go home
options: Stressed: it, up and and; nothing is linked
Stressed: every word; links only at the end
Stressed: pick, go and home; linked: “pick-it-up”; “and” reduced to /n/ in between
Stressed: pick and home; links only between go and home, and nowhere else
quests.correctAnswer: Stressed: pick, go and home; linked: “pick-it-up”; “and” reduced to /n/ in between
quests.hint: Content words carry the beats; the other words fall between them and link.
quests.explanation: “Pick”, “go” and “home” are the content words, so they carry the beats. “It up and” falls between “pick” and “go”: the /k/ links to “it” and the /t/ to “up”, and “and” is reduced to /n/. So the first half sounds like one chunk, “pi-ki-tup-n”.
quests.phoneticRule: Phrasal verbs with “it” link into one chunk, and the following “and” is reduced, so the stretch before the next beat is compact.

quests.instruction: Which description fits “Rita, write it up and send it”?
quests.word: Rita, write it up and send it
quests.textToSpeak: Rita, write it up and send it
options: Beats on Rita, write and send; “it up and” and “it” are squeezed and linked
Beats on every word, with no squeezed words and no linking between any of them
Beats on it, up and it, with “write” squeezed between the weak words
Two beats only, with the small words dropped and nothing linked
quests.correctAnswer: Beats on Rita, write and send; “it up and” and “it” are squeezed and linked
quests.hint: Find the three stressed words, then check which consonants link to vowels.
quests.explanation: The beats fall on “Rita”, “write” and “send”. The /t/ of “write” links to “it” and the /t/ of “it” links to “up”, “and” is reduced, and the final “it” links to “send” with its /d/: “sen-dit”. So rhythm and linking together give a smooth chain.
quests.phoneticRule: The chain of weak words around a stressed verb is both compressed and linked, so the verb phrase sounds like a single unit.

quests.instruction: A learner says “Dina wants to go to the shop” with a full vowel and equal stress on every word. What is the likely effect on listeners?
quests.word: Dina wants to go to the shop
quests.textToSpeak: Dina wants to go to the shop
options: It sounds more natural, because every word is clear
It makes the sentence ungrammatical
It has no effect on listeners at all, because they hear each word separately and clearly
The rhythm is lost, so the sentence sounds stiff and the key words are harder to find
quests.correctAnswer: The rhythm is lost, so the sentence sounds stiff and the key words are harder to find
quests.hint: Think about how listeners decide which words matter when everything has the same weight.
quests.explanation: Listeners use stress to find the key words. When every word has the same weight, the beats disappear and the sentence sounds slow and mechanical. It is not wrong, but it is harder to follow and tiring to listen to. Using weak forms is part of being clear, not less clear.
quests.phoneticRule: Equal stress on all words removes the rhythmic cues that listeners use to locate content words, reducing intelligibility and naturalness.
quests.spokenForm: DIna WANTS tuh GO tuh thuh SHOP

quests.instruction: Which spoken version of “Gina is going to the shop” keeps natural rhythm?
quests.word: Gina is going to the shop
quests.textToSpeak: Gina is going to the shop
options: “GI-NA IS GO-ING TO THE SHOP”: every syllable stressed equally, like a list of syllables
“GIna is GOing to the SHOP”: beats on the content words, small words squeezed
“Gina GOING SHOP”: all small words removed
“GINA is going TO THE SHOP”: stress on the function words
quests.correctAnswer: “GIna is GOing to the SHOP”: beats on the content words, small words squeezed
quests.hint: Choose the version that has strong content words and light small words.
quests.explanation: The natural version has beats on “Gina”, “going” and “shop”, and the small words “is”, “to” and “the” are squeezed. Removing small words changes the grammar, and stressing them hides the meaning. The goal is balance: strong content words, quiet function words.
quests.phoneticRule: Natural rhythm keeps all the words but gives the content words prominence and compresses the function words.
quests.spokenForm: GIna iz GOing tuh thuh SHOP

quests.instruction: How can you practise English rhythm with the sentence “Lena wants some tea and toast”?
quests.word: Lena wants some tea and toast
quests.textToSpeak: Lena wants some tea and toast
options: Say each word separately with a long pause between each of them
Tap the beats on the content words (Lena, wants, tea, toast) and fit the others between the taps
Say all the words at exactly the same length and the same loudness
Whisper the content words and shout the small words, so that the small words become the beats
quests.correctAnswer: Tap the beats on the content words (Lena, wants, tea, toast) and fit the others between the taps
quests.hint: Rhythm practice should make the content words stand out and the small words fit between them.
quests.explanation: Tapping the beats on the content words gives you a steady pulse, and you fit the small words between the taps. After a few repetitions you speed up. This trains you to hear the same pattern in other people’s speech and to produce it yourself.
quests.phoneticRule: Beat-tapping practice with content-word stress builds the stress-timed pattern by treating function words as fillers between beats.
quests.spokenForm: LEna WANTS sum TEA n TOAST

quests.instruction: Which words compress most in “Yara forgot to bring the tickets”?
quests.word: Yara forgot to bring the tickets
quests.textToSpeak: Yara forgot to bring the tickets
options: “to” and “the”, squeezed between the beats on “forgot”, “bring” and “tickets”
“forgot” and “tickets”, which are the longest words
“Yara” and “bring”, because they are short
No word, because every word is stressed equally in any formal sentence of English
quests.correctAnswer: “to” and “the”, squeezed between the beats on “forgot”, “bring” and “tickets”
quests.hint: Apply the rhythm test: which words carry the meaning, and which are only joiners?
quests.explanation: The beats fall on “Yara”, “forgot”, “bring” and “tickets”. The two small words “to” and “the” are squeezed into the gaps and weakened: /tə/ and /ðə/. Length does not decide compression; function is the deciding factor.
quests.phoneticRule: Compression depends on grammatical function, not word length: function words compress, and content words keep their beats.
quests.spokenForm: YAra forGOT tuh BRING thuh TICkets

quests.instruction: Which pattern fits “Jonah, where did you put the keys?”
quests.word: Jonah, where did you put the keys
quests.textToSpeak: Jonah, where did you put the keys
options: Beats on every word, so “did you” and “the” are fully and separately pronounced
Beats on Jonah and keys only, with all other words dropped
Beats on where, put and keys; “did you” (often blended) and “the” are squeezed between them
